title: Fighting the Anchoring Bias in Negotiations
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership examines anchoring bias, the cognitive phenomenon in which the first offer in any negotiation disproportionately shapes all subsequent counteroffers. Once an opening number is placed on the table, it functions as a psychological mooring: most negotiators counter in proximity to the anchor rather than from an independent assessment of true value. The newsletter urges leaders and professionals to recognize the anchor's power and counter it through deliberate reanchoring strategies or systematic reframing that refuses to let the opening offer define the scope of negotiation. The practical upshot is that whoever goes first implicitly gains an advantage, and skilled negotiators either lead with a strong number or explicitly refuse to let the first proposal constrain their position.
points: The first offer in a negotiation becomes a psychological anchor that constrains all subsequent counteroffers, regardless of its basis in actual value.
Anchoring bias operates even when negotiators are aware of it: knowing about the anchor does not neutralize it -- only deliberate reanchoring strategies can counter it.
Skilled negotiators don't accept the frame of the opening offer: they treat it as written in pencil and insist on exploring the full range of options before moving toward a number.
Going first can be an advantage if done strategically: a strong, well-justified opening offer shifts the center of gravity in your favor before the other side has set expectations.
Leaders should train teams to identify anchoring in real time: whether negotiating salary, contracts, or budgets, recognizing the anchor in the moment is the prerequisite for countering it.
quotes: In what is known as 'anchoring bias,' the first offer or proposal in a negotiation becomes a psychological mooring that sets the baseline.
Even though people can counter with whatever they choose, most people allow this anchor to define the parameters of the exchange.
Even if the team member were convinced that $160,000 reflects the true market value, they normally won't ask for that salary because of the anchor.
The anchoring bias exists in nearly all negotiations, so it is critical to remember that whoever offers the first proposal implicitly sets the tone for the negotiation.
Good negotiators don't let the opening proposal dictate their approach. They insist on exploring all the options available as if the opening offer were written in pencil, not ink.
